## Twelve children learning to talk

Between 1998 and 2001, researchers in Manchester recorded twelve English children at home, playing and talking with their mothers: an hour at a time, twice in every three-week period, from around each child's second birthday until around their third. The children are known by first names: Anne, Aran, Becky, Carl, Dominic, Gail, Joel, John, Liz, Nicole, Ruth and Warren.

This is the **Manchester corpus** (Theakston, Lieven, Pine & Rowland, 2001). It was collected to test the theory you read this week: that children build grammar verb by verb — and it is publicly available through [CHILDES](https://childes.talkbank.org), the international database of child language.

Everything the children and mothers said was transcribed. We have converted those transcripts into one table, where **each row is one utterance**: one thing one person said at one moment.

| column       | what it contains                                            |
|----------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `child`      | which child's recording this is (`"Anne"`, `"Becky"`, ...)  |
| `age_months` | the child's age at that recording, in months                |
| `speaker`    | who is talking: `"CHI"` (the child) or `"MOT"` (the mother) |
| `utterance`  | what they said                                              |
| `num_tokens` | how many words that is                                      |

So the row `Anne · 26 · CHI · "want some juice" · 3` means: Anne, aged 2;2, said *want some juice*: three words.

:::: {.predict-check data-answer="speaker" data-accept="the speaker column||speaker column"}
The mothers talk a lot in these recordings. Which column would you use to keep only the *children's* utterances?

::: pc-explanation
`speaker`: filtering for `speaker == "CHI"` keeps the child's own speech. `child` tells you *whose recording* it is; even in Anne's files, half the rows are her mother.
:::
::::

## Download the data

<a class="btn btn-primary" href="../data/manchester_utterances.rds" download> ⬇ manchester_utterances.rds</a>

This is an `.rds` file: R's own format for saving a data frame exactly as it is, types and all. Download it, then upload it into your working folder on UCloud: drag it into the Files pane, or use the Upload button there.

## Load it

``` r
# Load the tidyverse.
library(tidyverse)

# Read the data file into a variable called manchester.
manchester <- readRDS("manchester_utterances.rds")
```

Select the lines and press *Shift+Enter*. If R complains that the file does not exist, the file and your session are in different folders. Check the Files pane.

Now have a first look:

``` r
# glimpse() shows every column, its type, and the first few values.
glimpse(manchester)
```

``` repl
Rows: 597,644
Columns: 6
$ child      <chr> "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne", "Anne…
$ file       <chr> "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "011007", "0110…
$ age_months <dbl> 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 22, 2…
$ speaker    <chr> "CHI", "MOT", "CHI", "CHI", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "MOT", "CHI", "MOT",…
$ utterance  <chr> "baby", "here's baby", "it", "it fit", "baby willn't fit", "is it too big", "what about this baby look", "wanna put them on t…
$ num_tokens <int> 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 6, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 6, 3, 2, 1, 6, 7, 5, 1, 2, 4, 2, 1, 2, 2, 8, 9, 3,…
```

Note the types: `<chr>` means text, `<int>` means whole numbers. `speaker` and `utterance` are text; `age_months` and `num_tokens` are numbers you can compute with.

:::: {.callout-note .predict icon="false" title="🤔 Think first"}
`num_tokens` says how many *words* an utterance has. Someone had to decide what a word is. Does *don't* count as one word or two? Does a laugh count? Last Friday you made decisions exactly like this about turns.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Check your thinking"}
There is no neutral answer. Our rule: anything separated by spaces is a word, so *don't* is one, and laughs and unintelligible stretches don't count at all. Different rules would give different numbers in everything you compute today. That isn't a flaw; it's what measurement is.
:::
::::

## How much data is there?

`count()` from Tuesday tells you what each child contributes:

``` r
# Count the number of rows for each child.
manchester %>%
  count(child)
```

``` repl
# A tibble: 12 × 2
   child       n
   <chr>   <int>
 1 Anne    58403
 2 Aran    53900
 3 Becky   52512
 4 Carl    49030
 5 Dominic 60162
 6 Gail    46595
 7 Joel    52378
 8 John    35178
 9 Liz     37767
10 Nicole  51065
11 Ruth    57962
12 Warren  42692
```

The totals differ a lot between children. And one thing to know about `age_months`: because ages are rounded to the month, a busy month can contain *two* recording sessions bundled together. Raw counts reflect the recording schedule as much as the child. Keep that in mind; it will matter when we start comparing sessions.
